newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish leaders give conflicting growth estimates.
newsitem.headline: Turkish leaders give conflicting growth estimates.

text.p: Turkish leaders' conflicting estimates for Turkey's 1997 economic growth target led to confusion in the markets, economists said on Thursday.
However bankers and economists still rely on the official target set by the country's State Planning Organisation.
Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller gave Turkey's Gross National Product (GNP) growth target at around seven percent.
"We hope that we will attain our target which is around seven percent," Ciller told a meeting in Ankara.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has said: "This year the rate of growth will reach 14 percent."
Turkey's official target, unveiled in October under 1997 budget which was approved by parliament in December without any revision, was four percent.
Planning officials say they have not revised any economic target since then. "We stick with our target," said a planning official who declined to be named.
State Minister Ufuk Soylemez, in charge of the treasury, confirmed that the target was still four percent.
A senior private bank economist said conflicting estimates, supplied by senior government members, weakened the reliability of official targets.
"But I think the most reliable estimate is still the one made by the State Planning Organisation after a series of econometric modelling and long-lasting studies," the economist said.
Bankers say above-target growth rate in 1996 could have encouraged Erbakan and Ciller to make ambitious growth estimates.

"But Erbakan and Ciller will lower their estimates when they see that the economy is not growing as much as they expected. There is no early indication that Turkey will attain higher growth rate this year," the economist said.
Turkey's 1996 GNP growth is estimated at around 7.5 percent, sharply up from the official target of 4.5 percent.
But economists believe the economy slowed down in the final quarter of 1996 and is expected to grow at a slower pace in the first half of 1997.

Turkey's industrial output fell 0.2 percent in December, down from 5.5 percent in November, according to the most recent official data. The industrial growth rate was 15.7 percent in the same 1995 month.

Neither Erbakan nor Ciller have given any estimates on other key economic targets -- current acccount and inflation. Turkey has set its targets for 1997 current account deficit at $5.6 billion and year-on-year inflation at 58 percent.
Any upward deviation in the 1997 growth rate may make these targets unattainable as they were set under the assumption that the economy would grow four percent this year.
